name: Italy

position.summary: Meloni's government became the longest-serving postwar Italian government, but stability came under simultaneous pressure. ISTAT confirmed a 3.1% budget deficit for 2025, complicating Meloni's public claim that Italy would return below the 3% EU threshold in 2026. A new school decree capping classrooms at 30% students with insufficient Italian-language skills and banning full face coverings became the dominant domestic culture-war flashpoint. Salvini called an extraordinary League congress amid internal factional pressure, while Roberto Vannacci's breakaway far-right party faced its first serious parliamentary test. Bank consolidation rumors involving UniCredit, Credit Agricole, Intesa Sanpaolo, and Banco BPM circulated widely. Intesa's Fideuram unit confirmed a roughly 95-million-euro loss to an AI impersonation fraud. Eni announced pump-price cuts and the government convened refiners ahead of winter. The Senate gave final approval to nuclear power after decades without new reactors. Italy lost 0-2 to Belgium in Mancini's second match as national coach, with boos at a half-empty Stadio Olimpico. The Colosseum closed after a worker fell to his death during maintenance. Naples police seized 3.2 million euros hidden inside residential walls and furniture. A critical-minerals memorandum was signed between Rubio and Tajani.

key_events.event: School decree on veils and foreign-student caps enacted, triggering a culture-war confrontation across the coalition and opposition.
ISTAT confirmed a 3.1% budget deficit for 2025, straining Meloni's 2026 sub-3% pledge.
Vannacci's breakaway far-right party entered its first serious parliamentary test, pressuring Meloni's right flank.
Intesa Sanpaolo's Fideuram unit lost approximately 95 million euros to an AI impersonation fraud.
Italy lost 0-2 to Belgium in Mancini's second fixture, intensifying doubts about the rebuild.
The Colosseum closed after a maintenance worker fell to his death, prompting a safety review.
The Senate gave final approval to a nuclear-power law, ending decades of political stalemate on reactors.

Bank consolidation rumors and the Fideuram fraud put Italian banking at the centre of economic headlines.
Italy's 0-2 loss to Belgium and Mancini's fragile position make football the emotional barometer of national mood.

The school decree on veils and foreign students gets formally published and immediately draws legal challenges and protests, becoming the week's dominant domestic story. The 3.1% deficit keeps the bond market on edge, nudging BTP yields higher as Meloni publicly defends the 2026 sub-3% target. Mancini faces a make-or-break Nations League match and the naive reading takes the worst-case branch: Italy loses and his position is publicly challenged. Bank consolidation rumors heat up with at least two banks confirming exploratory talks around Banco BPM. The Colosseum reopens within the week, accompanied by a published safety review or capacity restriction, giving Rome a mixed relief-and-scrutiny narrative. No formal government collapse, no bank mega-merger, no Red Sea shock; the week is defined by pressure management rather than crisis.

display.headline: Meloni defends government amid school decree, deficit, and right-flank pressure
emoji_reasons: The core story is a sitting government managing simultaneous political, fiscal, and coalition pressures.
The 3.1% deficit and bond-market credibility question anchor the economic dimension.
Mancini's make-or-break Nations League fixture gives football a disproportionate role in the week's narrative.
display.tldr: Meloni's government survives the week under triple pressure from a culture-war school decree, a 3.1% deficit testing her 2026 fiscal credibility, and right-wing rivals Salvini and Vannacci. Bank consolidation rumors, a nuclear implementation debate, and Mancini's fragile football position complete a busy but non-crisis week.
